sources.title: Taiwanese semiconductor giant TSMC restarts operations after earthquake, easing concerns of chip supply disruption - Electronics Manufacturing News
sources.snippet:
The world’s largest independent contract chip manufacturer, which supplies 90 per cent of the world’s most advanced semiconductors to technology giants like Apple and Nvidia, restarted operations within 10 hours after work was suspended because of the worst earthquake to hit Taiwan in 25 years. There were at least nine fatalities and more than 1,000 injured during the earthquake. [...] Following a brief suspension of work, TSMC said 70 per cent of its chip-manufacturing equipment had been “recovered” for production at its fabrication facilities within 10 hours of the earthquake. New facilities, such as its Fab 18, achieved a recovery rate of more than 80 per cent. [...] Widespread concern about the state of Taiwan’s semiconductor manufacturing industry after the earthquake shows the pivotal role that TSMC and other major chip makers in the island play in the global technology supply chain. The island produces 60 per cent of the world’s semiconductors.

Analysts at Barclays initially warned that the production of certain chips in Taiwan could take weeks to recover, according to a note published on Wednesday.

brief.criticality_summary: High severity disruption affecting multiple semiconductor POs with low runway; immediate re‑routing needed to avoid production stop.

recommended_actions.title: Reroute MCU‑X200 supply to EuroSemi GmbH
recommended_actions.rationale: Highest value PO (€2.4M) with 10.9‑day runway; alternative supplier available to secure supply.

recommended_actions.title: Reroute MAT‑L10 microcontroller to EuroSemi GmbH
recommended_actions.rationale: Lowest runway (3.2 days) risk of stockout; alternative supplier ready to prevent line stop.

recommended_actions.title: Expedite Power Module L34 shipments
recommended_actions.rationale: Accelerate incoming shipments to buffer while alternative sourcing is arranged.

challenges.explanation: 100% of rerouted order value (€2,680,580) lands on EuroSemi GmbH; a problem there would recreate the exposure.
challenges.suggested_fix: Confirm the alternative's spare capacity before approving, or split volume across a second qualified supplier.

challenges.explanation: The plan assumes that switching to EuroSemi GmbH can happen immediately, ignoring required supplier qualification, PPAP approval, customs clearance, and logistics lead times. If these steps take weeks, the reroute will not prevent stockout.
challenges.suggested_fix: Add a qualification workstream: confirm EuroSemi’s PPAP status, estimate lead time for first article inspection, and qualify interim safety stock or dual‑source options. Include realistic timelines in the mitigation schedule.

challenges.target: Reroute to EuroSemi GmbH for MCU‑X200 and MAT‑L10
challenges.explanation: Both critical POs are diverted to the same alternative supplier without verifying EuroSemi’s current capacity or existing commitments. Overloading EuroSemi could create a new bottleneck and delay deliveries.
challenges.suggested_fix: Request capacity confirmation from EuroSemi for the additional volume, and if limited, split the load between EuroSemi and another approved alternate or consider using safety stock from existing inventory.

challenges.explanation: The plan relies on Evidence C4 claiming TSMC recovery within ten hours, but no source or validation is provided. If the disruption lasts longer, expediting alone may be insufficient.
challenges.suggested_fix: Obtain a verified timeline from TSMC or industry sources, and add a contingency (e.g., additional safety stock or alternate power‑module supplier) should the outage exceed the ten‑hour window.
